title: Docker
description: Run containers, publish ports, debug with logs and exec, and build your own images.

body.text: An image is a read-only package: an app plus everything it needs to run. A container is a running copy of an image. One image can start many containers.
Think of the image as a recipe and the container as the dish you cooked from it.
Getting an image

body.caption: Download the nginx web server image, then list local images

body.text: Without a tag, Docker uses :latest. In real projects pin a version, such as nginx:1.27, so builds stay repeatable.

options: A running copy of an image
A file that describes how to build an image
A virtual machine with its own kernel
correctAnswers: A running copy of an image
questions.explanation: Containers are started from images. A Dockerfile describes a build, Docker Hub stores images, and containers share the host's kernel instead of having their own.

questions.prompt: You can start several containers from the same image.
questions.explanation: The image never changes, so you can start as many containers from it as you like.

questions.prompt: Type the command that downloads the redis image.
questions.explanation: docker pull downloads an image from a registry such as Docker Hub.

questions.prompt: Type the command that lists the images on your machine.
questions.explanation: docker images (or docker image ls) lists downloaded and built images.

labs.title: Download your first image
labs.scenario: Before you can run a web server, you need its image on this machine.
hints: Images come from a registry. There is a docker command that downloads one.
Use docker pull with the image name, then list what is stored locally.
Type: docker pull nginx, then docker images

body.text: docker run starts a container from an image. -d runs it in the background and --name gives it a name you can remember.

body.code:
docker run -d --name web nginx
docker ps

body.text: Ports
A container has its own network. -p host:container publishes a port, so -p 8080:80 sends traffic from port 8080 on your machine to port 80 inside the container.
docker ps shows running containers. Add -a to also see stopped ones.
When a container misbehaves, its logs are the first place to look.

body.code:
docker logs web
docker logs -f web   # keep following new lines

body.text: docker exec runs a command inside a running container. With -it you get an interactive shell.

body.code:
docker stop web
docker rm web
body.caption: Stop the container, then remove it

questions.explanation: docker ps shows only running containers. Adding -a also shows stopped ones, and docker images lists images, not containers.

questions.prompt: In docker run -p 8080:80 nginx, which number is the port on your own machine?
questions.explanation: The format is host:container. 8080 is on your machine and 80 is inside the container.

questions.prompt: The -d flag deletes the container when it stops.
questions.explanation: -d means detached: the container runs in the background. The flag that removes it on exit is --rm.

questions.prompt: Type the command that shows the logs of a container named api.
questions.explanation: docker logs prints what the container wrote to its output. Add -f to keep following.

questions.prompt: Which flag gives a container a name you choose?
questions.explanation: --name web lets you write docker logs web instead of a random id. --tag is for images, -p for ports.

labs.title: Run your first container
labs.scenario: Start the nginx web server in the background and make it reachable on port 8080 of this machine.
hints: You need the nginx image first, then a running container with a published port.
docker run -d starts it in the background. -p host:container publishes a port.
Type: docker pull nginx, then docker run -d --name web -p 8080:80 nginx

labs.title: Check on a running container
labs.scenario: A container called web is already running. Find it, read its logs and open a shell inside it.
hints: Start by listing the running containers to confirm the name.
docker logs shows a container's output. docker exec runs a command inside it.
Type: docker ps, docker logs web, docker exec -it web sh

body.text: A container has its own network and its own files. Two things connect it to your machine: published ports and volumes.
Ports
-p host:container publishes a port: traffic to the host port is passed to the port inside the container.

body.code:
docker run -d -p 8080:80 nginx   # open localhost:8080
docker run -d -p 8081:80 nginx   # a second copy

body.text: Two containers cannot share a host port. Change the number on the left; the right one stays the port the app listens on.
Volumes
Files written inside a container are lost when the container is removed. A volume keeps them outside the container.

body.caption: The database files survive docker rm

body.text: This simulator accepts -v but does not store volume data. Real Docker keeps it in the named volume, here pgdata.

questions.prompt: One nginx container already uses host port 8080. How do you start a second one?
questions.explanation: Change the host port (left). nginx still listens on 80 inside its container.

questions.prompt: Without a volume, files a container wrote are still there after docker rm.
questions.explanation: Removing a container removes its files. Keep data that matters in a volume.

questions.prompt: Type the command that runs redis in the background and publishes port 6379 on the same host port.
questions.explanation: -d runs it in the background and -p 6379:6379 publishes the port.

labs.title: Two web servers
labs.scenario: A web container already uses port 8080. Start a second nginx called web2 on port 8081, then check that both are running.
hints: docker ps shows which host ports are already taken.
Run nginx again with -d, --name web2 and a free host port. The host port is the left number in -p.
Type: docker run -d --name web2 -p 8081:80 nginx, then docker ps

body.text: A Dockerfile is the recipe for your own image. Each line is one instruction, read from top to bottom.
FROM picks the base image. COPY puts your files inside. RUN runs a command while building, for example to install packages. EXPOSE notes the port, and CMD sets what starts when a container runs.
Build and run

body.code:
docker build -t mysite .
docker run -d -p 8080:80 mysite

body.text: -t gives the image a name (a tag). The dot means: use the Dockerfile in this folder.
Put lines that rarely change at the top. Docker caches each step, so rebuilding after a small change is fast.

questions.prompt: Which instruction comes first in a Dockerfile?
questions.explanation: FROM chooses the base image everything else builds on.

questions.prompt: In docker build -t mysite ., what does the dot mean?
options: Use the Dockerfile in this folder
correctAnswers: Use the Dockerfile in this folder
questions.explanation: The last argument is the build context: the folder Docker reads the Dockerfile and files from.

questions.prompt: Type the command that builds an image called api from the Dockerfile in this folder.
questions.explanation: -t names the image; . is the current folder.

labs.title: Build your own image
labs.scenario: Your website file is ready. Write a Dockerfile based on nginx, build an image called mysite and run it on port 8080.
hints: There is no editor here: write the Dockerfile with echo and > or >>. It must start with FROM nginx.
docker build -t mysite . builds from the Dockerfile in this folder. Then start it with docker run -d -p 8080:80.
Type: echo "FROM nginx" > Dockerfile, echo "COPY index.html /usr/share/nginx/html/" >> Dockerfile, docker build -t mysite ., docker run -d -p 8080:80 mysite
